prompt: For an octahedral complex that substitutes by a limiting dissociative (D) mechanism, which factor should NOT influence the stereochemical outcome?

choices.text: The identity of the leaving group
The identity of the entering group
choices.why: The section lists the entering group as an appropriate consideration. It reacts with the five-coordinate intermediate, so it can affect the product.

choices.text: The structure of the five-coordinate intermediate
choices.why: This is the main influence. In a D reaction, the product's structure depends primarily on the intermediate and how the entering ligand meets it.

choices.text: Whether the conditions are acidic or basic
choices.why: Conditions matter: under basic aqueous conditions, the conjugate base mechanism can change the stereochemical outcome.

explanation: In the purely dissociative case, the complex completely loses one ligand to become a five-coordinate intermediate. The leaving group is gone before the product forms, so its identity should not influence the outcome. The product depends mainly on the structure of the intermediate and its interaction with the entering ligand, and the reaction conditions (such as basic solution, where the conjugate base mechanism operates) also matter.

prompt: An octahedral complex loses a ligand in a D reaction. How does the geometry of the five-coordinate intermediate affect the stereochemistry of the product?

choices.text: A square pyramidal intermediate gives retention of configuration; a trigonal bipyramidal intermediate changes the configuration of at least some of the product
A trigonal bipyramidal intermediate gives retention; a square pyramidal intermediate changes the configuration of at least some of the product
choices.why: This is reversed. In a square pyramid, the entering ligand takes the site the leaving group vacated, so the configuration is kept.

choices.text: Both geometries always give complete retention of configuration
choices.why: Only the square pyramid gives retention. A trigonal bipyramid lets the entering ligand come in from several directions, so some product changes configuration.

choices.text: Both geometries give the same mixture of rearranged products
choices.why: The two geometries differ: the square pyramid keeps the original stereochemistry, while the trigonal bipyramid gives at least some rearranged product.

explanation: In general, if the intermediate is square pyramidal, the incoming ligand enters at the same site where the leaving group was lost, and stereochemistry is retained from reactant to product. If the intermediate is a trigonal bipyramid, at least some of the product will not retain the original configuration.

prompt: Square pyramidal and trigonal bipyramidal geometries usually have similar energies and readily interconvert by pseudorotation. Why is this interconversion normally ignored for the intermediate of a D reaction?

choices.text: The intermediate exists for such a short time that interconversion is assumed not to occur, unless it is unusually long-lived
The trigonal bipyramid is always much higher in energy than the square pyramid
choices.why: The section says the two geometries typically have similar energies. The reason is time, not energy.

choices.text: Five-coordinate metal complexes can only be square pyramidal
choices.why: Five-coordinate complexes can adopt either geometry. The whole analysis of D reactions compares the two.

choices.text: The entering ligand binds before the leaving group departs, so no five-coordinate species forms
choices.why: That would describe an associative pathway. In a D reaction the leaving group is lost first, giving a true five-coordinate intermediate.

explanation: Square pyramidal and trigonal bipyramidal geometries typically have similar energies and readily interconvert through pseudorotation. During a D reaction, though, the intermediate exists for such a short moment that interconversion is assumed not to occur, unless the intermediate is unusually long-lived. So the geometry the intermediate adopts sets the stereochemistry of the product.

prompt: When trans-[M(en)2LX]^{n+} loses X, rearranging to a trigonal bipyramid with L in an equatorial position needs only a 30° movement from any ligand. How far, in degrees, must one of the en nitrogens move to give the trigonal bipyramid with L axial instead?
explanation: A trigonal structure with axial L requires one en nitrogen to move by 90°, three times the 30° needed for equatorial L. Because it distorts the original ligand positions less, the trigonal bipyramid with equatorial L is the dominant one, even though the equatorial positions are slightly closer to the metal and more sterically hindered than the axial position.

prompt: In the dominant trigonal bipyramidal intermediate from trans-[M(en)2LX]^{n+}, L is equatorial and the entering ligand Y can attack from three directions along the equatorial plane. How many different stereoisomeric products can form, counting optical isomers separately?
explanation: Y entering trans to L gives the trans product. Y entering at either position cis to L gives cis-Λ or cis-Δ. That makes three optical isomers: trans, cis-Λ and cis-Δ.

prompt: Optically inactive trans-[M(en)2LX]^{n+} reacts through the trigonal bipyramid with L equatorial, and Y attacks from each of the three equatorial directions with equal probability. What product mixture is expected?

choices.text: Cis and trans product in a 2:1 ratio, with the cis product a racemic mixture of Λ and Δ
Cis and trans product in a 1:2 ratio, with the cis product a racemic mixture of Λ and Δ
choices.why: Only one of the three directions puts Y trans to L. The other two give cis product, so cis outnumbers trans 2:1.

choices.text: Cis and trans product in a 2:1 ratio, with the cis product a single enantiomer
choices.why: The two cis directions give Λ and Δ with equal probability, so an optically inactive reactant gives a racemic cis product.

choices.text: Only trans product, because Y always enters where X left
choices.why: That is the outcome of a square pyramidal intermediate. The trigonal bipyramid also gives cis products.

explanation: Y entering trans to L gives the trans product; Y entering at either site cis to L gives cis-Λ or cis-Δ. The two cis isomers are equally likely and form as a racemic mixture from the optically inactive trans reactant. The expected cis:trans ratio is 2:1.

prompt: Why does the conjugate base mechanism make a trigonal bipyramidal intermediate, with the deprotonated ligand in an equatorial position, more likely?

choices.text: The deprotonated ligand is a stronger π donor, and π donors prefer equatorial positions because π-donor interactions involve shorter bonds
The deprotonated ligand is a weaker π donor, so it moves to the less crowded axial position
choices.why: Deprotonation makes the ligand a stronger π donor, and π donors prefer the equatorial positions.

choices.text: The deprotonated ligand becomes a π acceptor, which prefers equatorial positions
choices.why: The section describes the deprotonated ligand as a stronger π donor, not a π acceptor.

choices.text: In basic solution the intermediate lives long enough to pseudorotate into the more stable form
choices.why: The intermediate is still assumed to be too short-lived to interconvert. The preference comes from the π donor favoring an equatorial site.

explanation: π-donor ligands prefer the equatorial positions of a trigonal bipyramid because of the shorter bond lengths involved in π-donor interactions. The deprotonated ligand produced by the conjugate base mechanism is a stronger π donor, so it favors an equatorial position. Even where a square pyramid is typically preferred, the conjugate base mechanism can tip the balance toward a trigonal intermediate.

prompt: Under acidic conditions, trans-[Co(en)2LCl]^+ gives 50% trans product for L = Br^− and 65% for L = Cl^−. These match neither the 100% expected from a square pyramidal intermediate nor the 33% expected from the equatorial-L trigonal bipyramid. What is the best explanation?

choices.text: The products come from a mixture of intermediates, each contributing to a different extent
In a D reaction, the identity of the leaving group changes the stereochemistry
choices.why: The leaving group is gone before the product forms, so it should not influence a D reaction. Here it is Cl^− in every case anyway.

choices.text: The trigonal bipyramid with L axial is the only intermediate
choices.why: Axial L is the less likely trigonal bipyramid, because forming it distorts the original ligand positions more. A single intermediate rarely explains the data.

choices.text: The cis products slowly isomerize back to trans after the reaction
choices.why: Nothing in the section suggests the products rearrange afterward. The ratios reflect which intermediates the reaction passes through.

explanation: The actual proportion of products of a given stereochemistry depends on the extent to which each possible intermediate leads to products. The percentages expected from any single intermediate are rarely found in experimental data; especially for trans-en complexes, product ratios result from mixtures of intermediates.

prompt: In trans-[Co(en)2LCl]^+, Cl^− is replaced by H2O under acidic conditions or by OH^− under basic conditions. The % trans product (acidic, basic) is: L = OH^−: 25, 6; Br^−: 50, 100; NH3: 100, 24; NO2^−: 100, 94. For which L does switching to basic conditions cause the largest loss of trans stereochemistry?

choices.text: NH3
OH^−
choices.why: Its trans product does fall, from 25% to 6%, but that is a drop of only 19 points. NH3 falls from 100% to 24%.

choices.text: Br^−
choices.why: For Br^−, basic conditions raise the trans product from 50% to 100%.

choices.text: NO2^−
choices.why: NO2^− keeps nearly all its trans stereochemistry: 100% in acid and 94% in base.

explanation: With L = NH3, the reaction is completely stereoretentive under acidic conditions (100% trans) but gives only 24% trans product under basic conditions, a drop of 76 points. Under basic conditions the conjugate base mechanism is possible; the deprotonated ligand it produces is a stronger π donor that favors a trigonal bipyramidal intermediate, which gives cis product.

prompt: Under acidic conditions, cis-[Co(en)2LCl]^+ complexes give 100% cis product for every L tested. What does the section conclude from this?

choices.text: They react only through a square pyramid, since the ligand trans to Cl^− is a non-π-donor en amine
They react through a trigonal bipyramid with L equatorial, because L is a strong π donor
choices.why: A trigonal bipyramid would give some rearranged product. The cis ligand L has no influence on the outcome under acidic conditions.

choices.text: The cis ligand L controls the outcome, holding the intermediate in its original shape
choices.why: The section states that L, cis to the leaving group, has no influence on the outcome under acidic conditions.

choices.text: The intermediate is long-lived enough to pseudorotate back to the original configuration
choices.why: The intermediate is assumed too short-lived to interconvert. Complete retention points to a square pyramidal intermediate.

explanation: In every cis-[Co(en)2LCl]^+ complex, the ligand trans to the leaving Cl^− is an amine nitrogen of en, which is not a π donor. So the cis isomer, unlike the trans, reacts exclusively through the square pyramidal intermediate under acidic conditions, and the product keeps the reactant's stereochemistry. The cis ligand L has no influence on the outcome under these conditions.

prompt: Under basic conditions, optically pure Δ-cis-[Co(en)2(NO2)Cl]^+ reacts with OH^− to give 46% Δ-cis, 20% Λ-cis and 34% trans product. What percentage of the product has a cis geometry?
explanation: Both Δ-cis (46%) and Λ-cis (20%) are cis: 46 + 20 = 66%. The other 34% is trans. Under basic conditions, where the conjugate base mechanism is possible, cis stereochemistry is not entirely retained, and the cis products come out in roughly a 2:1 Δ:Λ ratio from a Δ reactant (46:20 here).

prompt: Optically pure tris(acac)cobalt(III) carries a CD3-labeled acetyl group in an "outside" position, adjacent to the coordinating groups. As the complex racemizes, the labeled group moves to the "inside" position, directly coordinated to the metal. What does this show?

choices.text: The isomerization goes through bond breaking and bond re-forming steps
The isomerization goes by a twist, with no bonds broken or formed
choices.why: A twist doesn't break or make bonds, so it couldn't swap which group is coordinated to the metal.

choices.text: The cobalt changes oxidation state during the isomerization
choices.why: Nothing in the experiment involves redox. The label moving from outside to inside shows metal–ligand bonds breaking and re-forming.

choices.text: The labeled ligand can coordinate in only one way
choices.why: The labeled ligand is ambidentate, with different possible modes of coordination. That is what lets the label move inside.

explanation: This kind of rearrangement is essentially a substitution in which the leaving group and entering group are the same ligand. Isotopically labeled ambidentate ligands provide the evidence: the CD3-labeled acetyl group moves from an outside position to the inside, coordinated position as the optically pure complex becomes a racemic mixture. That change can only occur through bond breaking and re-forming steps.

prompt: How does a Bailar or Ray-Dutt twist interconvert isomers of an octahedral tris- or bis-chelate complex?

choices.text: One triangular face rotates relative to the opposite face, passing through a trigonal prismatic geometry, without breaking or forming bonds
One chelate arm dissociates and then re-binds at a different site
choices.why: That is the bond breaking and re-forming pathway. Twisting involves no bond breaking or bond forming.

choices.text: One triangular face rotates relative to the opposite face, passing through a trigonal antiprismatic intermediate
choices.why: The octahedron itself is the trigonal antiprism. Rotating a face until the two faces are eclipsed gives a trigonal prism, the intermediate.

choices.text: A Bailar twist breaks a metal–ligand bond, while a Ray-Dutt twist does not
choices.why: Neither twist breaks bonds. They differ only in the relationship between the chelate rings and the faces twisted.

explanation: An octahedron is a trigonal antiprism with all edge lengths identical. Rotating one triangular face relative to its opposite until the two are eclipsed gives a trigonal prism, and continuing the rotation gives another octahedral complex, so the trigonal prism is an intermediate in the isomerization. In tris- and bis-chelates, these are Bailar or Ray-Dutt twists, which differ only in the relationship between the chelate rings and the faces twisted.
